1.content: Share Go components and build optional native providers for QuickGUI. An extension can be an ordinary Go package that composes QuickGUI components, or a Go package backed by a separately built native library. Start with Go when the existing UI and platform APIs cover your feature. Add a native provider when you need an optional native dependency, as the terminal and updater packages do.
1.keywords: extension authoring init-extension zig rust plugin native provider third-party purego manifest ABI ServiceApi RequireExtension InvokeExtension OpenExtension npm

2.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Choose an extension type
2.content: What you are adding What you ship Core changes Components, themes, or application logic A Go module None A native service, SDK, or optional backend A Go package, manifest, and native library implementing the service ABI None UI backed by native data A native service plus Go components using existing primitives None Native services register automatically by name. Use your own Go module, npm package or scope, and release cycle. Consumers import your Go package; the CLI discovers its manifest and bundles the selected native artifact. No core registry entry, provider-specific kind, CLI fork, or QuickGUI release-pipeline change is needed. An extension runs in the application's process. The Go application loads the core and selected providers through purego. Each provider owns its backend dependencies; the core keeps the renderer, layout engine, and native event loop. Go edits reuse these libraries, so consumers do not rebuild the native backend on every edit.

3.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Create an extension project
3.content: go is the default and creates a reusable component with a reactive demo. zig , rust , and moonbit create a standalone native service with a typed Go wrapper, a manifest, vendored ABI definitions, and an npm artifact package. Every template includes cmd/demo and quickgui.toml : Use --module github.com/acme/my-service for your Go module and --npm-package @acme/my-service-native for a native artifact package. --name overrides the directory-derived extension name. Defaults are example.com/<name> and <name>-native . --no-install skips bun install and go mod tidy ; initialization preserves non-empty directories. The Zig template requires Zig 0.16.x; Rust uses stable Cargo/Rust. Build scripts are TypeScript run with Bun. bun run build builds the native library for the current machine into artifacts/lib/<target>/ . The manifest supplies its identity and release version to the Go wrapper, generated native constants, and npm package. bun run dev builds it once, then reuses it while watching Go edits. Restart after editing native code. Pure Go extensions have no native build step or artifact package. Before the packages are published, use bun packages/cli/src/cli.ts init-extension <directory> --type <type> --no-install from this checkout. Set the generated Go SDK requirement to the local go directory with a replace directive and the CLI dependency to a local file: path, then install dependencies. The generated README describes development and publishing. For moonbit , implement operations in native/extension.mbt using MoonBit and a native C compiler. The Bun script compiles through MoonBit's C backend and links a private runtime into the shared library; the Go application still loads it through purego. No core changes or Go toolchain are needed to build the provider alone. See MoonBit extension authoring for the handler API, memory ownership, toolchain setup, and use from either frontend.

4.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Share a Go component
4.content: Create a module under your own repository path, depend on the Go SDK, and export component functions. This package needs neither a native manifest nor an npm package: Call notice.Notice(message, ui.Style{Padding: 16}) inside a component or children block. The accessor stays reactive, and the caller's style merges after the defaults. Component functions declare children without returning a node. Use ui.OnCleanup for resources owned by a mounted component; keep application-wide services outside component ownership. Publish the module using Go version tags, and document the SDK versions you support. Consumers add it with go get using your module path. Transitive imports of terminal or updater still opt the application into those native extensions, so keep optional integrations in separate packages or build-tagged files.

5.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Lay out a native extension
5.content: The working native-extension example pairs a Go package with a small C library named acme-echo . It builds against the standalone C ABI header , with no renderer or core crate dependency. In your own repository, use a layout such as: Vendor the small header into your project. C, C++, Rust, and other languages that export a C ABI can implement a provider. Rust providers can vendor the equivalent extension_api.rs layouts and build a cdylib , without linking quickgui , quickgui-host , WGPU, or Taffy. The updater backend demonstrates an asynchronous service. The provider in this guide uses its own release 1.0.0 . Its descriptor, manifest, npm package, and RequireExtension version must agree. The service ABI version and table layout determine core compatibility; the provider's release does not need to match QuickGUI's release. Document the Go SDK and service ABI versions your package requires. The built-in terminal's typed rendering contract remains tied to its matching core release.

6.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Declare the Go dependency
6.content: Place this manifest beside the imported Go package's source , not just at the module root or in application configuration: Names start with a lowercase letter and contain at most 64 lowercase letters, digits, or hyphens. Choose a distinctive name; host is reserved and terminal uses its built-in typed contract. The library field is quickgui_ plus the name with hyphens replaced by underscores, without lib or a file extension. The npm package may use any valid scope or be unscoped. The manifest is limited to 16 KiB, and an application can require at most 32 providers. The Go package declares the matching release during initialization and exposes a typed operation: RequireExtension only records a requirement. Do not load libraries, open windows, or start workers in init . Call operations after native.Run reports readiness, on the UI goroutine. Replies also run there. native.InvokeExtension sends any JSON-encodable value and returns the provider's JSON result, preserving explicit null members. Methods start with an ASCII letter and contain up to 64 ASCII letters, digits, dots, underscores, or hyphens. For a persistent service, call native.OpenExtension(name, options, changed, ready) and wait for its successful ready callback. Use session.Request("lookup", value, done) for a JSON result, or session.Command when only an error is needed. Each command has its own reply; events remain subscribed until session.Close() . Close on the UI goroutine when the owner is disposed. Reserve start and stop for session lifecycle. Wrap these low-level calls with typed options, events, and methods in your public package. The CLI discovers manifests through go list -deps , using the same entry package, target, and build tags as compilation. Transitive imports count; excluded files do not. Both the manifest and the RequireExtension call are needed: one controls bundling, the other controls loading.

7.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Implement the native contract
7.content: Export quickgui_extension_v1 with C linkage and default symbol visibility. It returns a static descriptor containing your name, exact provider version, ABI version 1 , service kind 2 , and a two-function table. All services share this kind; do not invent a new kind per provider. The public header defines every field and callback signature. A Rust service implements ServiceApi.invoke and ServiceApi.shutdown . This descriptor fragment uses a local copy of the ABI definitions: Only C layouts, fixed-width fields, borrowed byte spans, and function pointers cross the boundary. Keep language-owned objects and allocator ownership inside their library. The descriptor, strings, and table have static lifetimes. Copy borrowed request bytes before retaining them, enqueue slow work, and return immediately. Do not wait for network I/O, worker completion, or native main-thread execution. Bound queues, active sessions, and retained data; catch recoverable panics before crossing an extern "C" boundary. The Go session protocol is: Request Parameters Provider responsibility A one-shot method such as echo The value passed to InvokeExtension Reply once, then release its sink start The options JSON passed to OpenExtension Use the request ID as the session ID; reply and retain its event sink A command such as send {"session": 123, "value": "hello"} Find that session and settle this command's own reply stop {"session": 123} Stop accepting work for that session, cancel its resources, and reply shutdown function No parameters Cancel all sessions without blocking the UI thread ServiceSink.emit kind 0 carries one successful JSON reply, kind 1 a UTF-8 error, and kind 2 a JSON session event. Use null for success without a result. Request and emitted payloads are each limited to 64 KiB. Payload bytes are borrowed only during emit ; the host copies them into its existing event queue. Workers may emit from any thread. Schedule OS APIs that require the main thread on that thread without blocking the calling Go goroutine. The start sink stays alive after the start reply so it can deliver events. Command sinks are separate. Call each sink's release exactly once, including errors and rejected work, after its final callback. Closing a session must suppress later events and release workers; keeping a library loaded must not keep its sessions alive. Extension images remain loaded for process lifetime because callbacks may still reference their function pointers. The C echo implementation shows the complete one-shot contract. For visual features, publish changed data to reactive Go components built from existing QuickGUI primitives. The service ABI does not add custom renderer node kinds; a new rendering primitive still requires a renderer implementation.

8.content: Before application startup, the Go loader opens each selected image, calls its exported entry point, and passes the descriptor and required version to the core. The core validates the header before reading its layout, then checks the name, release, ABI, table size, and non-null callbacks. It stores service tables by name and automatically routes extension/acme-echo/<method> requests and application shutdown. Identical registrations are idempotent. Different versions or tables under the same name are rejected, and the CLI also rejects conflicting npm packages under that name. Provider callbacks run outside the registry lock. The registry and loaded images persist for the process lifetime; your shutdown function must cancel all remaining sessions. There is no provider-specific registry code to edit.

9.hierarchy: Authoring Extensions › Build and package artifacts
9.content: Use TypeScript scripts run with Bun to build native artifacts once. The example's build-extension.ts compiles its C provider directly with Clang and stages the current host target. A Rust provider can invoke Cargo from its own repository in the same way: Set the Rust library name to quickgui_acme_echo and its crate type to cdylib . Run bun build-extension.ts on each supported host. This script does not cross-compile. Target directories are darwin-arm64 , darwin-x64 , linux-arm64 , linux-x64 , windows-arm64 , and windows-x64 . Ship only targets you build and validate. The native npm package contains artifacts and exposes its metadata for the resolver: Replace @acme with your own scope. Publish this artifact package with your own release workflow and keep it optional; the Go import selects it. Your build script and releases are independent of QuickGUI's built-in --extension command and version synchronization. Consumers reuse your prebuilts during Go edits. If your provider needs helper executables or resources, declare their basenames in a manifest resources object keyed by darwin , linux , or windows . Each platform accepts up to 16 distinct files; the same platform list applies to both architectures. Put those files next to the library in every applicable target directory. The CLI copies them alongside the native libraries and marks plain resource executables as executable. Directory resources use .qgr bundles produced by the repository's packResources helper. It preserves executable modes and confined relative symlinks with entry and byte limits. Resource paths cannot overwrite core or provider images. macOS frameworks must also satisfy the platform's signing requirements. Sparkle resources receive the existing macOS signing and bundle configuration; other services do not need updater settings.

10.content: Try the standalone example from a QuickGUI checkout: For your own consumer, add your Go module with go get , import its package, and run quickgui dev or quickgui build . Install the matching native npm package for offline or private distribution, or let the CLI fetch the exact release from the public npm registry. For development, set QUICKGUI_EXTENSION_DIR to the absolute target artifact directory. This override must contain every required library and resource, including transitive requirements. Resolution checks the explicit directory, installed npm package, then exact-version npm download; source-checkout fallback applies only to QuickGUI's built-in packages. Downloads require SHA-512 integrity, only declared artifacts are extracted, and caches include the npm package identity. Private registry downloads are not automatic; install private packages with your package manager first. Before shipping, verify these behaviors: An app without the import bundles no provider or optional backend dependencies. Adding and removing a transitive import changes a fresh bundle correctly. The bundled executable loads the provider through purego with the matching core. Missing files, names, ABI versions, release versions, and conflicting requirements produce errors. Starting, closing before startup finishes, repeated closing, cancellation, and application shutdown release every callback context and worker. Events stop after disposal. Background work never blocks the UI. Clean sessions sleep; queues, snapshots, caches, and resource payloads have limits. Follow the performance guide . bun pm pack includes every library and resource your manifest declares. Install the resulting archive into a separate consumer, build with native source staging unavailable, and exercise it on each supported OS and architecture. The repository's scripts/check-extensions.ts builds the independent C provider, exercises its real replies through purego, and bundles a separate consumer with its own Go module and npm scope. It also checks the built-in providers and their combinations. Add equivalent checks to your extension repository. End users receive the packaged application with all selected libraries; they need no Bun, Cargo, npm packages, or native toolchain to run it.

11.content: Add optional Sparkle-compatible updates to a Go application. The optional github.com/egoist/quickgui/go/updater package provides automatic application updates. Importing it includes @quickgui/native-updater ; apps without the import include neither that library nor Sparkle. Ordinary Go edits reuse the prebuilt native artifacts.
11.keywords: updater sparkle appcast ed25519 extension updates

12.content: Generate an Ed25519 key pair with Bun tooling: Keep the private .key outside version control and copy the contents of .pub into quickgui.toml : The CLI embeds the current version, identifier, target-specific feed URL, default preference, and public key in the Go executable. On macOS it also generates Sparkle's Info.plist settings and signs the nested Sparkle helpers with the app's identity. Secret keys are never embedded. Developer ID apps are supported; App Store and sandboxed builds must exclude the updater import using a Go build tag or platform file.

13.content: Start after native.Run reports readiness, outside components. Share the handle between settings, menus, and any update banner. An updater belongs to the application, so closing a window must not close it. Call updates.Check(done) from a Check for Updates menu item, updates.Install(done) from an available-update banner, and updates.SetAutomaticChecks(enabled, done) from settings. Callbacks always run on the Go UI goroutine. State() reads the latest cached event without calling native code or polling. Initialization and commands report errors through their completion callbacks. Options can override the feed URL and public key. Windows/Linux also allow current version and identifier overrides; Sparkle reads those from the app bundle, and its public key must match the embedded SUPublicEDKey . Development builds are disabled by default, including when using a release-built native library. Use AllowDevelopment: true only with a deliberately configured test feed and disposable app bundle.

14.content: Event.Status is idle , checking , available , downloading , installing , or disabled . Events include version, plain-text notes, progress byte counts, the automatic-check preference, and an optional error. An explicit check that finds no update reports Kind == "up-to-date" on the portable backend. macOS also uses Sparkle's standard result windows. On macOS, scheduled discoveries are retained for an in-app banner. Manual checks promote a retained result into Sparkle's standard UI. Sparkle owns download, verification, installation, scheduling, and relaunch. Its persisted preference takes precedence over the packaged default. Windows and Linux perform one quiet check per launch when enabled, and another when automatic checking is enabled. There is no idle polling timer. Download progress is throttled to at most ten events per second plus completion. Checks and installation cannot overlap; an explicit check adopts an in-flight automatic check. The portable installer verifies the artifact before preparing a handoff. QuitRequired means the helper has validated its inputs and is waiting for the current process to exit. Call native.App.Quit(false, nil) after dealing with unsaved work. If quit is cancelled, the helper times out after two minutes and leaves the current application intact. Closing an updater cancels checks and pre-handoff downloads; an accepted installer handoff is already owned by the helper.

15.content: Platform Update payload Installation macOS ZIP containing the signed .app Sparkle 2.9.4, embedded only with the extension Windows QuickGUI NSIS .exe installer A helper waits for app exit, runs the verified installer with /S and the current install directory, then relaunches Linux Type-2 .AppImage A helper waits for app exit, replaces the user-owned AppImage atomically, and restores the old image if replacement or startup fails Linux .deb , system binaries, unpacked AppDirs, and root-owned installations report disabled ; use their package manager. A new AppImage must retain the updater import so the SDK can acknowledge startup to the helper. Linux backups are deleted only after that acknowledgement and a short startup grace period. Windows installer failures are reported; rollback remains the installer's responsibility. The portable backend supports HTTPS Sparkle RSS appcasts, raw Ed25519 enclosure signatures, semantic-version ordering, target-specific feeds, and Windows minimum-system requirements. It skips deltas and unsupported channel/rollout constraints. It does not implement every Sparkle feature. Feed reads are limited to 1 MiB, downloads to 512 MiB, and presentation notes to 16 KiB. Signatures and declared lengths are checked again by the installer helper before installation. No unsigned fallback is available.

16.content: Place the private key in QUICKGUI_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY (or SPARKLE_PRIVATE_KEY ), using your CI secret store. Alternatively, updates.ed25519SecretKey points to a local key file. Keys use Sparkle's current base64-encoded 32-byte Ed25519 seed format and also work with Sparkle's sign_update tool. The CLI signs the finished platform artifact and writes appcast-<target>.xml . Upload the versioned artifact first, then replace the feed at its configured HTTPS URL. Feeds are per target, so architectures cannot accidentally install each other's binaries. The generated feed contains the current release; it does not generate Sparkle delta archives or staged rollouts. updates.manifest = true enables generation for every production build. macOS archives preserve framework symlinks and should contain the Developer ID signed, notarized app. Windows requires makensis ; sign the installer with the configured Authenticode identity. Linux requires appimagetool to produce an updateable AppImage. Public-key mismatches, missing signing keys, missing installers, and unsupported payloads fail the build. Existing Rust users can explicitly enable the legacy updater Cargo feature for the Minisign JSON UpdateClient . It is no longer a default feature or part of the Go native core. That legacy client and its CLI manifest path remain separate from this Sparkle-compatible extension; use updater.Start , not the removed native.Updater facade.

17.content: The builder stages the shared library plus Sparkle resources on macOS, or the installer helper on Windows/Linux. The CLI discovers the import transitively and fetches the exact-version extension package when necessary. End users need only the packaged application. The current npm release matrix ships macOS artifacts. Windows/Linux implementations can be built from source on their target hosts; publishing those prebuilt targets follows the framework's broader platform release support. See the runnable example and native extension contract . Sparkle configuration and appcast details are documented by Sparkle .

The prebuilt native library is loaded in the same process through purego. Bun runs the CLI for development and packaging.

30.content: Every component uses func() , including window roots, routes, conditional branches, and children blocks. It declares zero or more children without returning a node. Components run once when mounted. UI calls inside a children block attach to that block’s parent. Use normal Go if and for for static construction; use ui.Show or ui.For when a signal must change the child structure.

31.content: Pass an accessor for changing text or properties. Calling count() while constructing a string captures its current value; placing the call in func() string keeps it reactive. Event handlers batch writes automatically. Use ui.Batch for a group of writes elsewhere, and ui.CreateMemo for derived values. String and numeric signals can be children directly: ui.Text("Count: ", count) . The prefix stays retained while only the number updates. Numeric bindings use strconv ; they do not parse a format string. For a combined string property, use strconv.Itoa(count()) and concatenation inside an accessor.

32.content: WindowOptions.Component creates one reactive root per window. Closing the window disposes its nodes and effects. Register resource cleanup with ui.OnCleanup . For background work, ui.Async delivers its result back to the UI goroutine and cancels when its component is disposed.

33.content: Capture native.CurrentWindow() while the component is mounting, then use the captured window in callbacks. Do not look it up from an unrelated goroutine. Window events and native requests expose asynchronous callbacks.

34.content: Declare routes with ui.Route and ui.Layout . A layout mounts its matched child with ui.Outlet . Read parameters with ui.UseParams , or navigate with ui.UseRouter .

36.content: Multiple style records merge field by field in order. A later record only overrides fields it declares, including nested Hover , Active , and other interaction styles. Shared records are never mutated. Numeric lengths are logical pixels; strings also accept percentages. Zero is an explicit value; nil omits a field. Run bun run fmt to format long calls consistently.

41.content: Add Transition to the base style to animate changes between paint states. See Transitions & Animation for hover effects, signal-driven changes, timing, and reduced motion. Use Hover: &ui.Style{...} , Active , Focus , Disabled , and Selected for interaction styles. ui.When merges its records while the condition is true and restores the earlier fields when it turns false. Only affected bindings update; children remain mounted.

42.hierarchy: Styling & Layout › Groups and named group hover
42.content: ui.Group(true) marks an unnamed hover group; ui.Group("card") names it. A descendant’s GroupHover: &ui.Style{...} follows its nearest ancestor group, including named groups. ui.GroupHoverNamed("card", ...) follows the nearest ancestor with that name, skipping intervening groups with other names. Hovering any part of the group, including its padding and descendants, activates its rules. A nested group becomes the target for unnamed rules; named rules can still follow an outer group. With no matching ancestor, the rule has no effect. Repeated group rules accumulate in declaration order; a node’s own Hover wins for overlapping properties. Use paint properties such as colors, opacity, outlines, and transforms. Hover updates are handled natively without rerunning components or changing layout. GroupActive: &ui.Style{...} and ui.GroupActiveNamed("card", ui.Style{...}) follow pressed groups. FocusWithin: &ui.Style{...} follows focus in the node or a descendant. These states accept paint styles and cannot set the cursor.

43.content: Animate native style changes and images with retained Go components. Animate changes to retained nodes with ui.Style{Transition: ...} . The native runtime advances the frames; your component does not rerun for every frame. Import ui from github.com/egoist/quickgui/go/ui .
43.keywords: transition animation easing duration hover opacity reduced motion gif webp

44.content: Put the transition on the base style so it applies when the pointer enters and leaves. The same declaration works with other paint states, including Active , Focus , Expanded , and DragOver .

45.content: Use a signal or ui.When to change the target. The card below keeps the same node and children while its color and opacity animate. Updating the target during a transition starts from its current visible value, including when reversing direction.

46.hierarchy: Transitions & Animation › Timing and frame rate
46.content: Use ui.TransitionDeclaration when several properties share one timing configuration. Import time for the duration in this example. The corresponding longhand fields can also be set directly in ui.Style{} : Field Usage TransitionProperty A comma-separated string or []string of supported property names. TransitionDuration Milliseconds as a number, a time.Duration , or a string such as "180ms" or "0.18s" . The host bounds durations to 0–10 seconds. TransitionEasing "linear" , "ease" , "ease-in" , "ease-out" , or "ease-in-out" . "ease" aliases the default "ease-in-out" ; these select QuickGUI curves. TransitionTimingFunction Alias for TransitionEasing . TransitionMaxFps Optional frame-rate cap. Omit it to follow display presentation; completion still occurs at the transition deadline. A node has one duration, easing, and frame-rate cap for all selected properties. Comma-separated shorthand entries collect property names; the last duration and easing apply to the entire list. Delays, cubic-bezier() , and independent timings per property are not supported. Explicit longhand fields override the shorthand. A duration alone, such as Transition: 180 * time.Millisecond , transitions background, border, and text colors. Select "all" explicitly to include all supported paint properties. Use Transition: "none" to remove the shorthand declaration.

47.content: Transition name Go style field background-color or background BackgroundColor or a solid Background border-color BorderColor border-width BorderWidth and edge widths border-radius BorderRadius and corner radii color Inherited Color opacity Subtree Opacity box-shadow BoxShadow transform Subtree Transform , including translation, scale, and rotation "all" means these properties. Gradient stops, width, height, padding, and other layout values do not interpolate through Transition . Unsupported transition property names are rejected. For a sliding switch thumb, use Transform: "translateX(20px)" and Transition: "transform 160ms ease-out" , then change the target to "translateX(0px)" when unchecked. This moves the painted subtree and its hit area without moving neighboring layout. Transforms interpolate their affine translation, scale, shear, and shortest rotation; TransformOrigin itself changes immediately. The Go UI API exposes paint transitions and animated images. CSS keyframes, timeline callbacks, and spring declarations are not Go style props.

48.hierarchy: Transitions & Animation › Mounting and reduced motion
48.content: A transition animates a change on an existing node; initial styles are applied directly. Keep the node mounted while changing its target. ui.Show removes its children when false and does not wait for an exit fade. Opacity zero alone keeps layout and input behavior. For dialogs, ui.DialogRootProps.EnterDuration and ExitDuration control transition completion and closing-content lifetime; OnOpenChangeComplete reports completion. Those durations do not create visual styles by themselves. See Dialog . Transitions respect the system's Reduce Motion preference. native.WindowOptions.ReduceMotion accepts a *bool for an explicit window policy; leave it nil to follow the system. Motion resolves to its target under Reduce Motion. Hidden or occluded windows pause local transitions, and completed transitions stop requesting frames.

49.content: Pass an animated GIF or WebP path to ui.Image . The native decoder retains the frames and the file's repeat policy; no Go timer or per-frame signal is needed. The path must resolve to an available file, or you can pass a data URL. Package file assets with the CLI's resources option. See Image and project configuration .

50.content: Choose between primitives and accessible compound components. QuickGUI combines unstyled primitives with accessible compound controls. Compose both through ordinary Go functions.

52.content: Compound families expose parts such as ui.Tabs.Root , ui.Tabs.List , and ui.Tabs.Panel . The core handles roles, keyboard navigation, focus, and control state. Create a part inside its root’s children callback so its context exists.

53.content: A controlled value is an accessor; its callback stores the value accepted by the control. Use a default value to let the component own its state. Optional scalar values use pointers, while multiple selections use slices.

Before application startup, the Go loader opens each selected image, calls its exported entry point, and passes the descriptor and required version to the core. The core validates the header before reading its layout, then checks the name, release, ABI, table size, and non-null callbacks. Different versions or tables under the same name are rejected, and the CLI also rejects conflicting npm packages under that name. Provider callbacks run outside the registry lock. The registry and loaded images persist for the process lifetime; your shutdown function must cancel all remaining sessions. There is no provider-specific registry code to edit.

Event.Status is idle , checking , available , downloading , installing , or disabled . Events include version, plain-text notes, progress byte counts, the automatic-check preference, and an optional error. An explicit check that finds no update reports Kind == "up-to-date" on the portable backend. macOS also uses Sparkle's standard result windows. On macOS, scheduled discoveries are retained for an in-app banner. Manual checks promote a retained result into Sparkle's standard UI. Sparkle owns download, verification, installation, scheduling, and relaunch. Its persisted preference takes precedence over the packaged default. Windows and Linux perform one quiet check per launch when enabled, and another when automatic checking is enabled. There is no idle polling timer. Download progress is throttled to at most ten events per second plus completion. Checks and installation cannot overlap; an explicit check adopts an in-flight automatic check. The portable installer verifies the artifact before preparing a handoff. QuitRequired means the helper has validated its inputs and is waiting for the current process to exit. Call native.App.Quit(false, nil) after dealing with unsaved work. If quit is cancelled, the helper times out after two minutes and leaves the current application intact. Closing an updater cancels checks and pre-handoff downloads; an accepted installer handoff is already owned by the helper.

Every component uses func() , including window roots, routes, conditional branches, and children blocks. It declares zero or more children without returning a node. Components run once when mounted. UI calls inside a children block attach to that block’s parent. Use normal Go if and for for static construction; use ui.Show or ui.For when a signal must change the child structure.

Export quickgui_extension_v1 with C linkage and default symbol visibility. It returns a static descriptor containing your name, exact provider version, ABI version 1 , service kind 2 , and a two-function table. All services share this kind; do not invent a new kind per provider. The public header defines every field and callback signature. A Rust service implements ServiceApi.invoke and ServiceApi.shutdown . This descriptor fragment uses a local copy of the ABI definitions: Only C layouts, fixed-width fields, borrowed byte spans, and function pointers cross the boundary. Keep language-owned objects and allocator ownership inside their library. The descriptor, strings, and table have static lifetimes. Copy borrowed request bytes before retaining them, enqueue slow work, and return immediately. Do not wait for network I/O, worker completion, or native main-thread execution. Bound queues, active sessions, and retained data; catch recoverable panics before crossing an extern "C" boundary. The Go session protocol is: Request Parameters Provider responsibility A one-shot method such as echo The value passed to InvokeExtension Reply once, then release its sink start The options JSON passed to OpenExtension Use the request ID as the session ID; reply and retain its event sink A command such as send {"session": 123, "value": "hello"} Find that session and settle this command's own reply stop {"session": 123} Stop accepting work for that session, cancel its resources, and reply shutdown function No parameters Cancel all sessions without blocking the UI thread ServiceSink.emit kind 0 carries one successful JSON reply, kind 1 a UTF-8 error, and kind 2 a JSON session event. Use null for success without a result. Request and emitted payloads are each limited to 64 KiB. Payload bytes are borrowed only during emit ; the host copies them into its existing event queue. Workers may emit from any thread. Schedule OS APIs that require the main thread on that thread without blocking the calling Go goroutine. The start sink stays alive after the start reply so it can deliver events. Command sinks are separate. Call each sink's release exactly once, including errors and rejected work, after its final callback. Closing a session must suppress later events and release workers; keeping a library loaded must not keep its sessions alive. Extension images remain loaded for process lifetime because callbacks may still reference their function pointers. The C echo implementation shows the complete one-shot contract. For visual features, publish changed data to reactive Go components built from existing QuickGUI primitives. The service ABI does not add custom renderer node kinds; a new rendering primitive still requires a renderer implementation.

Pass an accessor for changing text or properties. Calling count() while constructing a string captures its current value; placing the call in func() string keeps it reactive. Event handlers batch writes automatically. Use ui.Batch for a group of writes elsewhere, and ui.CreateMemo for derived values. String and numeric signals can be children directly: ui.Text("Count: ", count) . The prefix stays retained while only the number updates. Place the private key in QUICKGUI_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY (or SPARKLE_PRIVATE_KEY ), using your CI secret store. Alternatively, updates.ed25519SecretKey points to a local key file. Keys use Sparkle's current base64-encoded 32-byte Ed25519 seed format and also work with Sparkle's sign_update tool. The CLI signs the finished platform artifact and writes appcast-<target>.xml . Upload the versioned artifact first, then replace the feed at its configured HTTPS URL. Feeds are per target, so architectures cannot accidentally install each other's binaries. The generated feed contains the current release; it does not generate Sparkle delta archives or staged rollouts. updates.manifest = true enables generation for every production build. macOS archives preserve framework symlinks and should contain the Developer ID signed, notarized app. Windows requires makensis ; sign the installer with the configured Authenticode identity. Linux requires appimagetool to produce an updateable AppImage. Public-key mismatches, missing signing keys, missing installers, and unsupported payloads fail the build. Existing Rust users can explicitly enable the legacy updater Cargo feature for the Minisign JSON UpdateClient . It is no longer a default feature or part of the Go native core. That legacy client and its CLI manifest path remain separate from this Sparkle-compatible extension; use updater.Start , not the removed native.Updater facade.

Place this manifest beside the imported Go package's source , not just at the module root or in application configuration: Names start with a lowercase letter and contain at most 64 lowercase letters, digits, or hyphens. Choose a distinctive name; host is reserved and terminal uses its built-in typed contract. The library field is quickgui_ plus the name with hyphens replaced by underscores, without lib or a file extension. The npm package may use any valid scope or be unscoped. The manifest is limited to 16 KiB, and an application can require at most 32 providers. The Go package declares the matching release during initialization and exposes a typed operation: RequireExtension only records a requirement. Do not load libraries, open windows, or start workers in init . Call operations after native.Run reports readiness, on the UI goroutine. Replies also run there. native.InvokeExtension sends any JSON-encodable value and returns the provider's JSON result, preserving explicit null members. Methods start with an ASCII letter and contain up to 64 ASCII letters, digits, dots, underscores, or hyphens. For a persistent service, call native.OpenExtension(name, options, changed, ready) and wait for its successful ready callback. Use session.Request("lookup", value, done) for a JSON result, or session.Command when only an error is needed. Each command has its own reply; events remain subscribed until session.Close() . Close on the UI goroutine when the owner is disposed. Reserve start and stop for session lifecycle. Wrap these low-level calls with typed options, events, and methods in your public package. The CLI discovers manifests through go list -deps , using the same entry package, target, and build tags as compilation. Transitive imports count; excluded files do not. Both the manifest and the RequireExtension call are needed: one controls bundling, the other controls loading.
